title: The stricter sense of 'grace that makes pleasing'; is it charity?
source_text: XXI. Etenim sciendum est apud scriptores Ecclesiae Romanae, gratiam gratum facientem ordinarie sumi sensu longe strictiore, quam sumitur in modo allata divisione. Juxta quam ita opponitur gratiae gratis datae, ut sub se comprehendat omne donum internum, quod per se salutem accipientis juvat, atque ad eam dirigitur. Nam per gratiam gratum facientem intelligunt habitum & qualitatem quandam, per quam homo proprie & formaliter justus constituitur; adeoque simpliciter Deo gratus & amicus. De qua gratia multas inter se versant quaestiones, quarum haec praecipua est, An gratia illa sit habitus aliquis a charitate distinctus, an vero omnino idem cum charitate.
pass_a_gloss: XXI. For it is to be known that among the writers of the Roman Church, grace making pleasing is ordinarily taken in a sense far stricter, than it is taken in the division just brought. According to which it is so opposed to grace freely given, that it comprehends under itself every internal gift, which of itself helps the salvation of the receiver, and is directed to it. For by grace making pleasing they understand a habit and certain quality, by which man is properly and formally constituted righteous; and so simply pleasing and a friend to God. Concerning which grace they turn over many questions among themselves, of which this is the chief, Whether that grace is some habit distinct from charity, or rather altogether the same with charity.
pass_b_english: Thesis XXI. It should be understood that writers of the Roman Church ordinarily take the grace that makes pleasing in a far narrower sense than in the division just given. There it is set against grace freely given in such a way that it covers every inward gift that of itself helps the receiver's salvation and is directed to it.
In the narrower sense they mean by it a habit, a kind of quality, by which a man is properly and formally made righteous and so simply pleasing to God and his friend.
They debate many questions among themselves about this grace. The chief is whether it is a habit distinct from charity or entirely the same as charity.
